kodex.notes:
KODEX-1 does not hold up on the held-out messages. On the 20 odd messages (m01 to m39) it loses to en_terse on all 7 tokenizers. It still beats full English on all 7.

Ratio of KODEX tokens to en_terse tokens, held-out set (design set in brackets):
- o200k: 1.084 (0.837)
- cl100k: 1.180 (0.931)
- claude_legacy: 1.307 (1.027)
- llama3: 1.162 (0.926)
- llama4: 1.095 (0.824)
- mistral_tekken: 1.036 (0.815)
- mistral_sp: 1.178 (0.956)

Against full English the held-out ratio is 0.78 to 0.97. Out of 20 messages, KODEX is shorter than en_terse in 1 to 6, depending on the tokenizer.

How it was run:
- heldout_kodex.py imports attempt_1.evaluate() with config B_num10 rather than copying it. So form assignment, macro and number expansion, rendering and token counting are the original code.
- Check 1: the script first reruns the original even messages and stops unless the totals (340/379/413/377/336/349/437), all 20 rendered messages and attempt_1_spec.txt match exactly. They do.
- Check 2: it confirms every existing entry keeps its form.
- The 5 new entries were added after the last frozen entry, in order of first use. assign_forms gave them pool ranks 2399 to 2403, the next unused forms; the related-word filter skipped none. Each costs 1 to 2 tokens and they appear once each, so they are not why it loses.
- Adding them grows the spec by 11 to 17 tokens; the spec itself is 7,118 to 9,108 tokens and is not counted in the totals above.

Why it does not generalize (measured):
1. The phrase codebook was fitted to the even messages. Those used 19 phrase occurrences of 19 different phrases. The odd messages could use only 4 phrases, 6 times in total (so_far, keep_unchanged, open_pr, conf_high). Phrases saved 37 tokens (about 10%) on o200k on the design set but only 9 (about 2%) here.
2. The encodings got longer. The held-out set needs 407 forms against 442 en_terse tokens on o200k (0.92). The design set needed 312 against 406 (0.77).
3. Of the 229 entries used, 162 were never used on the design set.
4. The forms cost more than one token each on several tokenizers: 1.46 tokens per form on claude_legacy and 1.48 on mistral_sp.
5. Raw chunks such as URLs, file paths and Q1 names cost as much as in English, plus the quote marker.

Caveats:
- The encodings are mine and are not checked by a model; no model was available, so the back-translations have not been tested by a decoder.
- Some choices add forms for faithfulness: past-tense markers, extra sentence separators, an explicit subject after 'so', and 'branch X WITH fix' to avoid an imperative reading.
- Some paraphrases stretch the grammar: two POINTs in a version number, 'straight' for 'in a row', raw O(n^2) for 'quadratic', and dropping 'Please'.
- Every paraphrase is listed in the JSON; none of these choices changes the overall conclusion.

The JSON also holds per-message tokens, en and en_terse counts per message, wins and ties, totals for the other variants (with phrases expanded, rank-shuffled forms, raw digits), and spec token counts with and without the additions. The only files written are the two new ones; no existing file was changed.

lean.notes:
On the 20 held-out odd messages, LEAN (A_conservative) is longer than en_terse on all 7 tokenizers. Ratios vs en_terse: o200k 1.140, cl100k 1.248, claude_legacy 1.338, llama3 1.236, llama4 1.136, mistral_tekken 1.074, mistral_sp 1.281. On the even messages it was designed on, the same ratios were 0.84 to 1.04, and it was shorter than en_terse on 5 of the 7 tokenizers. It is still shorter than plain en on every tokenizer: 0.81 to 0.99 here, against 0.62 to 0.77 on the even set. Message by message, it is shorter than en_terse on only 1/20 (o200k), 1/20 (llama4) and 3/20 (mistral_tekken) messages, and on 0/20 for the other four tokenizers.

Why: it needs more words, not costlier ones. The odd encodings use 418 morphemes excluding raw spans, against 313 on the even set, while en_terse grows only from 406 to 442 tokens (o200k). The average tokens per morpheme is unchanged (o200k 1.038 on both sets; cl100k 1.165 vs 1.182). Workarounds drive the extra words:
- The LK linker is used 17 times here and 0 times on the even set.
- Function words are 40% of morphemes, against 29% on the even set.
- Frozen verb classes block common noun compounds: 'test', 'fix', 'limit' and 'search' are verbs, and 'report' is a noun. So "unit test", "rate limit", "the fix" and "the search" all need workarounds.
- A verb at the start of a clause is always read as the predicate.
- 'return' takes two objects and would swallow the next clause's noun phrase.
- 'BY' only means the agent ("by someone").
- The grammar has no 'yes', and its closed list of conjunctions has no 'unless'.

The six additions cost 6 to 12 tokens per tokenizer in total. Even if they were free, the verdict would not change.

Method:
- I used the frozen lexicon JSON rather than rebuilding it. a2_build sorts `set(D)`, so words with tied frequencies are ordered by Python's hash seed, and a rebuild swapped 68 domain-word forms. The script checks that the frozen JSON plus `a2_build.encode` reproduce the original even-message encodings and totals exactly.
- New entries get forms by continuing the build loop with the same skip rules. Every reading of "next unused form" gives the same forms, at positions 2501 to 2506.
- 126 existing entries had no class ('?') because no even message used them. I gave each the class needed here, one class per word, and did not change any class the even glosses had fixed. 'within' and 'near' became prepositions (P).

Faithfulness compromises:
- Two words are dropped: 'Please' in m01 (the request mode already marks a request) and 'Yes' in m35.
- m37 now states that I committed the fix, rather than just that the fix is on the branch.
- m19 says "I failed in the translation step" instead of "the translation step failed".
- I bent three grammar rules: a clause-boundary marker (PD) after a raw name followed by a noun in m33, a mode word right after 'so' in m25, and 'HTTP 503' written as a raw identifier.

Hazard: 4 frozen forms used here look like the start of another word in these same messages, which the original review rule would have blocked: cach (unit) vs cache, interf (key) vs interface, offic (stop) vs official, inst (d50) vs instead.

I judged faithfulness myself; with no model access, I could not check whether a model decodes these correctly.
